oggetti/orsa-maggiore/stelle/0/significa: The brightest star in Ursa Major, the first star of the Plough's handle.
oggetti/orsa-maggiore/stelle/1/significa: From the Arabic for 'bear'. An orange giant: together with Merak it points to the Pole Star.
oggetti/orsa-maggiore/stelle/2/significa: From the Arabic for 'the leader' or 'the guide'. It is the last star of the handle.
oggetti/orsa-maggiore/stelle/3/significa: From the Arabic for 'the belt'. Alcor sits right beside it: telling the two apart with the naked eye used to be an eyesight test.
oggetti/orsa-maggiore/stelle/4/significa: From the Arabic for the bear's 'loins'. Together with Dubhe it points to the Pole Star.
oggetti/cassiopea/stelle/0/significato: A nickname given by the American astronaut Gus Grissom: it is his middle name, Ivan, spelt backwards. It is a variable star.
oggetti/cassiopea/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic 'al-sadr', 'the breast'. It is an orange giant.
oggetti/cassiopea/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic 'al-kaff', 'the hand'. It is a white star.
oggetti/cassiopea/stelle/3/significato: From the Arabic for the queen's 'knee'.
oggetti/cassiopea/stelle/4/significato: A blue star at the end of the W.
oggetti/orione/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic 'rijl', 'the foot': it is the hunter's left foot. A blue-white supergiant.
oggetti/orione/stelle/1/significato: An Arabic name that reached us garbled by copying mistakes. A red supergiant: you can clearly see its orange colour, and its brightness changes over time.
oggetti/orione/stelle/2/significato: Latin for 'the female warrior'. It is the hunter's shoulder, on the opposite side from Betelgeuse.
oggetti/orione/stelle/3/significato: From the Arabic for 'the string of pearls': it is the star in the middle of the Belt.
oggetti/orione/stelle/4/significato: From the Arabic for 'the belt': it is the Belt star closest to Sirius.
oggetti/scorpione/stelle/0/significato: From the Greek for 'rival of Ares' (Mars), because its red colour is like the planet's. It is a huge red supergiant.
oggetti/scorpione/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the raised tail': it is the sting.
oggetti/scorpione/stelle/2/significato: A name of Sumerian origin. A yellow giant in the curve of the tail.
oggetti/scorpione/stelle/3/significato: From the Arabic for the scorpion's 'forehead'. A blue-white star that since 2000 has become a little brighter and variable.
oggetti/scorpione/stelle/4/significato: A name from the language of the Wardaman, an Aboriginal Australian people, adopted by the IAU in 2017. An orange giant.
oggetti/cigno/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic 'dhanab', 'tail': it marks the swan's tail. It is a white supergiant, extremely far away and far brighter than the Sun.
oggetti/cigno/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic 'sadr', 'breast': it sits at the centre of the cross.
oggetti/cigno/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic 'al-janah', 'the wing': it marks one of the swan's wings.
oggetti/cigno/stelle/3/significato: From the Arabic for 'the horsemen'. It marks the swan's other wing.
oggetti/cigno/stelle/4/significato: The name came about through a series of translation mistakes from Arabic into Latin in the Middle Ages. A small telescope shows it as a double: one golden star and one blue.
oggetti/leone/stelle/0/significato: From the Latin 'Regulus', 'little king', a name used by Copernicus. It lies almost on the ecliptic: every so often the Moon hides it.
oggetti/leone/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic 'al-jabhah', 'the forehead' (of the lion). Through a telescope it is a lovely double of golden stars.
oggetti/leone/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic 'dhanab al-asad', 'the lion's tail'.
oggetti/leone/stelle/3/significato: From the Greek for 'girdle'. It lies on the lion's back.
oggetti/costellazione-andromeda/cosa: A large autumn constellation. Its main stars form a line of three stars that starts from one corner of the Square of Pegasus.
oggetti/costellazione-andromeda/quando: Evenings from October to December, highest in November at around 9 pm.
oggetti/costellazione-andromeda/dove: From Italy it passes almost overhead, very high up. From the southern hemisphere it stays low on the northern horizon. To find it, start from Alpheratz, the top left corner of the Square of Pegasus.
oggetti/costellazione-andromeda/come: With the naked eye; under a dark sky you can see the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) as an elongated smudge, and it looks even better through binoculars.
oggetti/costellazione-andromeda/origine: Andromeda is a Greek name, that of the princess in the myth. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/costellazione-andromeda/storia: Andromeda was the daughter of Cepheus and Cassiopeia. She was chained to a rock as an offering to a sea monster (Cetus) and was rescued by Perseus. The galaxy M31 is about 2.5 million light years away: it is the most distant object you can see with the naked eye.
oggetti/costellazione-andromeda/stelle/0: From the Arabic 'mi'zar', 'girdle': it marks Andromeda's girdle. It is a red giant, orange in colour. From here you climb up towards M31.
oggetti/costellazione-andromeda/stelle/1: From the Arabic 'surrat al-faras', 'the horse's navel': it was once shared with Pegasus. It is the corner of the Square of Pegasus.
oggetti/costellazione-andromeda/stelle/2: From the Arabic name of a small desert wild cat, the caracal. Through a small telescope it is a beautiful double star, orange and blue.
oggetti/costellazione-andromeda/stelle/3: An orange star, halfway between Alpheratz and Mirach.
oggetti/macchina-pneumatica/cosa: A small, faint constellation with no recognisable shape. It lies below the long body of Hydra.
oggetti/macchina-pneumatica/quando: Evenings from March to May, highest in April at around 9 pm.
oggetti/macchina-pneumatica/dove: From Italy it stays low on the southern horizon, so you need a clear horizon. From the southern hemisphere it passes high in the sky, almost overhead.
oggetti/macchina-pneumatica/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky, far from towns, and binoculars help you find its few stars.
oggetti/macchina-pneumatica/origine: Antlia is Latin for 'pump': it is the pump for creating a vacuum, the air pump (in Italian, 'macchina pneumatica'). It was introduced by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in 1751-52.
oggetti/macchina-pneumatica/storia: Lacaille observed the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope, in South Africa, and filled the empty spaces with instruments of science and the arts. The vacuum pump was a famous instrument in physics experiments of the 17th and 18th centuries.
oggetti/macchina-pneumatica/stelle/0/sig: The brightest star, an orange giant. It has no proper name.
oggetti/macchina-pneumatica/stelle/1/sig: This one is also an orange star, just slightly fainter.
oggetti/macchina-pneumatica/stelle/2/sig: A faint star, visible only under a dark sky.
oggetti/uccello-del-paradiso/cosa: A small constellation near the south pole of the sky, made up of a few faint stars.
oggetti/uccello-del-paradiso/quando: It cannot be seen from Italy. From the southern hemisphere it is visible all year round, highest on July evenings.
oggetti/uccello-del-paradiso/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it never sets: it stays low towards the south, near the south celestial pole, below Triangulum Australe.
oggetti/uccello-del-paradiso/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky, far from towns; binoculars show the pair of delta stars nicely.
oggetti/uccello-del-paradiso/origine: Apus comes from the Greek 'apous', 'without feet'. It was introduced by the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman and published by Plancius at the end of the 16th century.
oggetti/uccello-del-paradiso/storia: It represents the bird of paradise, from New Guinea. The first skins that reached Europe had been prepared without legs, so people thought these birds had no feet and were always flying.
oggetti/uccello-del-paradiso/stelle/0/si: The brightest star, an orange giant. It has no proper name.
oggetti/uccello-del-paradiso/stelle/1/si: A yellow star, almost as bright as alpha.
oggetti/uccello-del-paradiso/stelle/2/si: An orange star close to gamma.
oggetti/acquario/cosa: A large zodiac constellation made of not very bright stars. The easiest part is the 'Water Jar': a little group of four stars in the shape of a Y.
oggetti/acquario/quando: Evenings from September to November, highest in October at around 9 pm.
oggetti/acquario/dove: From Italy it is halfway up the sky towards the south, below and to the right of the Square of Pegasus. From the southern hemisphere it passes high, almost overhead.
oggetti/acquario/come: With the naked eye under a dark sky; with binoculars you can find the globular cluster M2, which looks like a fuzzy little star.
oggetti/acquario/origine: Aquarius is Latin for 'the water carrier'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD), but it is much older: the Babylonians already knew it.
oggetti/acquario/storia: In Greek myth it is often Ganymede, the young man carried off by Zeus and taken to Olympus to pour drinks for the gods. Every year, between late July and August, the shooting stars of the Delta Aquariids seem to come from here.
oggetti/acquario/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic 'sa'd al-su'ud', 'the luck of lucks'. It is a yellow supergiant.
oggetti/acquario/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic 'sa'd al-malik', 'the luck of the king'. It lies almost exactly on the celestial equator.
oggetti/acquario/stelle/2/significato: Probably from the Arabic 'al-saq', 'the leg'. It gives its name to the Delta Aquariids meteor shower.
oggetti/aquila/cosa: A summer constellation shaped like a bird in flight. Its bright star Altair has two fainter stars beside it, one on each side.
oggetti/aquila/quando: Evenings from July to September, highest in August at around 9 pm.
oggetti/aquila/dove: From Italy it is high in the south. From the southern hemisphere it is halfway up the sky towards the north. Altair is one of the three corners of the Summer Triangle, together with Vega and Deneb.
oggetti/aquila/come: With the naked eye; binoculars show the Milky Way full of stars, and the star eta (η Aql) is a variable that changes brightness roughly every 7 days.
oggetti/aquila/origine: Aquila is the Latin name of the bird, the eagle. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/aquila/storia: In Greek myth it is the eagle of Zeus, which carried his thunderbolts. In another story it is the eagle that carried off the young Ganymede, who is Aquarius nearby.
oggetti/aquila/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic 'al-nasr al-ta'ir', 'the flying eagle'. It is about 17 light years away and spins very fast.
oggetti/aquila/stelle/1/significato: An orange giant. With Altair and beta it forms a short line of three stars that is easy to recognise.
oggetti/aquila/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic 'al-'uqab', 'the eagle'. It is a white star in the eagle's tail.
oggetti/aquila/stelle/3/significato: A blue-white star in the southern wing.
oggetti/altare/cosa: A small southern constellation shaped like an altar, with a compact little group of moderately bright stars. It lies below the tail of Scorpius.
oggetti/altare/quando: From Italy it is barely visible. From the southern hemisphere the best evenings are from June to August, highest in July at around 9 pm.
oggetti/altare/dove: From Italy it never rises; from Sicily and southern Italy you can glimpse part of it, skimming the southern horizon. From the southern hemisphere it passes high in the sky, below the tail of Scorpius.
oggetti/altare/come: With the naked eye; binoculars show the globular cluster NGC 6397, one of the closest to us.
oggetti/altare/origine: Ara is Latin for 'altar'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/altare/storia: In Greek myth it is the altar on which the gods of Olympus swore their alliance before the war against the Titans. The Milky Way running above it was seen as the smoke rising from the altar.
oggetti/altare/stelle/0/significato: An orange giant, the brightest star in the constellation along with alpha.
oggetti/altare/stelle/1/significato: A name of Chinese origin meaning 'pestle'. It is a blue-white star.
oggetti/ariete/cosa: A small zodiac constellation. With the naked eye you mainly see three stars in a slightly crooked line, below Andromeda.
oggetti/ariete/quando: Evenings from November to January, highest in December at around 9 pm.
oggetti/ariete/dove: From Italy it is high in the south, between the Pleiades and the Square of Pegasus. From the southern hemisphere it is halfway up the sky towards the north.
oggetti/ariete/come: With the naked eye; it has no bright objects, but gamma (Mesarthim) is a lovely double star for a small telescope.
oggetti/ariete/origine: Aries is Latin for 'ram'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/ariete/storia: In Greek myth it is the ram with the golden fleece that saved the siblings Phrixus and Helle; its fleece is the one sought by Jason and the Argonauts. More than 2000 years ago the Sun was in Aries at the spring equinox: that is why that point is still called the 'first point of Aries'.
oggetti/ariete/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic 'al-hamal', 'the ram'. It is an orange giant.
oggetti/ariete/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic 'al-sharatan', 'the two signs', because it is paired with gamma. It is a white star.
oggetti/ariete/stelle/2/significato: A name that comes from the astronomy of ancient India, where it referred to a group of stars in this area.
oggetti/ariete/stelle/3/significato: A small telescope splits it into two almost identical white stars.
oggetti/auriga/cosa: A winter constellation shaped like a large pentagon. Its star Capella is one of the brightest in the sky.
oggetti/auriga/quando: Evenings from December to February, highest in January at around 9 pm.
oggetti/auriga/dove: From Italy it passes almost overhead, above Orion and Taurus. From the southern hemisphere only part of it can be seen, low on the northern horizon.
oggetti/auriga/come: With the naked eye; with binoculars you can find three star clusters in a row, M36, M37 and M38, inside the pentagon.
oggetti/auriga/origine: Auriga is Latin for 'charioteer', the one who drives the chariot. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/auriga/storia: It is often identified with Erichthonius, king of Athens, who according to myth invented the four-horse chariot. He is drawn holding a she-goat (Capella) and her kids, three little stars close together.
oggetti/auriga/stelle/0/significato: From the Latin for 'the little she-goat'. It is about 43 light years away; in reality it is two yellow giant stars very close together.
oggetti/auriga/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the shoulder of the one holding the reins'. It is a double star that eclipses itself roughly every 4 days.
oggetti/auriga/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic for 'the wrist' (of the charioteer). It is a blue-white star.
oggetti/auriga/stelle/3/significato: An orange giant in the bottom corner of the pentagon.
oggetti/auriga/stelle/4/significato: A mysterious star: roughly every 27 years it is partly darkened, for almost two years, by a companion hidden in a disc of dust.
oggetti/boote/cosa: A large constellation shaped like a kite or an ice-cream cone. At the bottom is Arcturus, a very bright orange star.
oggetti/boote/quando: Evenings from May to July, highest in June at around 9 pm.
oggetti/boote/dove: From Italy it is very high, almost overhead. From the southern hemisphere only part of it can be seen, low in the north. To find Arcturus, follow the curve of the Plough's handle and keep going.
oggetti/boote/come: Arcturus is easy to spot with the naked eye, even in town; epsilon (Izar) is a lovely yellow and blue double, but you need a telescope.
oggetti/boote/origine: Boötes is a Greek name meaning 'herdsman', the one who drives the oxen. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/boote/storia: The herdsman seems to chase the Great Bear around the pole, and so he was seen as the bear's guardian. In its northern part there used to be a constellation that has since been abolished, Quadrans Muralis (the Mural Quadrant): the Quadrantid shooting stars of early January take their name from it.
oggetti/boote/stelle/0/significato: From the Greek 'Arktouros', 'the guardian of the bear'. It is an orange giant about 37 light years away, the brightest star in the northern half of the sky.
oggetti/boote/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the veil' or 'the girdle'. Through a telescope it is a double of different colours, also called 'Pulcherrima', 'the most beautiful'.
oggetti/boote/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic 'al-mufrid', 'the solitary one'. In the sky it is very close to Arcturus.
oggetti/boote/stelle/3/significato: A white star in the herdsman's shoulder.
oggetti/bulino/cosa: A tiny, faint constellation, little more than four small stars. It has no recognisable shape.
oggetti/bulino/quando: Evenings from December to February, highest in January at around 9 pm.
oggetti/bulino/dove: From Italy it is always very low, skimming the southern horizon, below Lepus and next to Columba. From the southern hemisphere it passes high, almost overhead.
oggetti/bulino/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky, far from towns, and a clear southern horizon; it has no objects suited to binoculars.
oggetti/bulino/origine: Caelum is Latin for 'burin' or 'chisel', the tool used to engrave metal. It was introduced by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in 1751-52.
oggetti/bulino/storia: Lacaille filled the southern sky with instruments of the arts and sciences. The burin was the engravers' tool; in those days they prepared the plates used to print star charts.
oggetti/bulino/stelle/0/significato: The brightest star, yellowish-white. It has no proper name.
oggetti/bulino/stelle/1/significato: An orange giant, with a faint companion visible through a telescope.
oggetti/bulino/stelle/2/significato: A faint star, visible only under a dark sky.
oggetti/giraffa/cosa: A large northern constellation, but made up only of faint stars. It fills the empty space between the Pole Star, Capella and Perseus.
oggetti/giraffa/quando: From Italy it never sets; it is highest on winter evenings, from December to February.
oggetti/giraffa/dove: From Italy it is high in the north, between Polaris and Capella. It cannot be seen from the southern hemisphere.
oggetti/giraffa/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky; with binoculars you can find 'Kemble's Cascade', a long line of little stars that ends at the cluster NGC 1502.
oggetti/giraffa/origine: Camelopardalis comes from Greek and means 'camel-leopard': that is what the ancients called the giraffe, tall like a camel and spotted like a leopard. It was introduced by the Dutch cartographer Petrus Plancius at the beginning of the 17th century.
oggetti/giraffa/storia: It has no Greek myth: it is a modern invention to fill a patch of sky with no constellations. According to a widely held explanation, Plancius was thinking of the camel on which Rebecca rode to marry Isaac, in the Bible.
oggetti/giraffa/stelle/0/significato: The brightest star, a yellow supergiant. It has no proper name.
oggetti/giraffa/stelle/2/significato: A very distant blue supergiant. It is a 'runaway star', racing quickly through space.
oggetti/cancro/cosa: A small, dim zodiac constellation between Gemini and Leo. At its centre is a star cluster, the Beehive.
oggetti/cancro/quando: Evenings from February to April, highest in March at around 9 pm.
oggetti/cancro/dove: From Italy it is high in the south, between Castor and Pollux and Regulus. From the southern hemisphere it is halfway up the sky towards the north.
oggetti/cancro/come: Through binoculars the Beehive (M44) is beautiful: a star cluster that, under a dark sky, looks like a little cloud to the naked eye.
oggetti/cancro/origine: Cancer is Latin for 'crab'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/cancro/storia: In Greek myth it is the crab sent by Hera to bite Hercules while he was fighting the Hydra; Hercules crushed it. More than 2000 years ago the Sun was in Cancer at the summer solstice: that is why the northernmost parallel where the Sun reaches the zenith is called the Tropic of Cancer.
oggetti/cancro/stelle/0/significato: The brightest star in Cancer, an orange giant.
oggetti/cancro/stelle/1/significato: From the Latin for 'the southern donkey'. It sits next to the Beehive, as if the donkeys were eating at the manger.
oggetti/cancro/stelle/2/significato: Through a small telescope it is a lovely double star, yellow and blue.
oggetti/cancro/stelle/4/significato: From the Latin for 'the northern donkey', the other donkey next to the Beehive.
oggetti/cani-da-caccia/cosa: A small constellation below the handle of the Plough. With the naked eye you see little more than two stars.
oggetti/cani-da-caccia/quando: Evenings from April to June, highest in May at around 9 pm.
oggetti/cani-da-caccia/dove: From Italy it is very high, almost overhead, just below the handle of the Plough. From the southern hemisphere only part of it can be seen, low in the north.
oggetti/cani-da-caccia/come: With the naked eye you can see Cor Caroli; with binoculars you can find the globular cluster M3, and with a telescope the famous Whirlpool Galaxy (M51).
oggetti/cani-da-caccia/origine: Canes Venatici is Latin for 'hunting dogs'. It was introduced by the Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius in 1687.
oggetti/cani-da-caccia/storia: Hevelius drew two dogs on Boötes' leash, which seem to be chasing the Great Bear. The two dogs are called Asterion and Chara.
oggetti/cani-da-caccia/stelle/0/signific: From the Latin for 'the heart of Charles', in honour of a king of England. Through a small telescope it is a double star.
oggetti/cani-da-caccia/stelle/1/signific: The name of one of the two dogs, from the Greek for 'joy'. It is a star similar to the Sun.
oggetti/cani-da-caccia/stelle/2/signific: A faint white star, on the border with Ursa Major.
oggetti/cane-maggiore/cosa: A winter constellation containing Sirius, the brightest star in the whole night sky. Its stars outline a standing dog.
oggetti/cane-maggiore/quando: Evenings from January to March, highest in February at around 9 pm.
oggetti/cane-maggiore/dove: From Italy it is low in the south. To find it, follow the three stars of Orion's Belt down and to the left: you will reach Sirius. From the southern hemisphere it passes high, almost overhead.
oggetti/cane-maggiore/come: Sirius is easy to spot with the naked eye, even in town; with binoculars, just below Sirius, you can find the star cluster M41.
oggetti/cane-maggiore/origine: Canis Major is Latin for 'greater dog'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/cane-maggiore/storia: In myth it is one of the hunting dogs of Orion the hunter, following him across the sky. In summer Sirius rises together with the Sun: this is where the Italian word 'canicola' comes from, meaning the hottest days of the year (in English, the 'dog days').
oggetti/cane-maggiore/stelle/0/significa: From the Greek 'seirios', 'scorching'. It is about 8.6 light years away and is the brightest star in the night sky.
oggetti/cane-maggiore/stelle/1/significa: From the Arabic for 'the virgins'. It is a very hot blue star.
oggetti/cane-maggiore/stelle/2/significa: From the Arabic for 'the weight'. It is a yellow supergiant much larger than the Sun.
oggetti/cane-maggiore/stelle/3/significa: From the Arabic for 'the herald': it rises shortly before Sirius and announces it.
oggetti/cane-maggiore/stelle/4/significa: A blue-white supergiant in the dog's tail.
oggetti/cane-minore/cosa: A tiny constellation: with the naked eye you can see only two stars, the very bright Procyon and Gomeisa beside it.
oggetti/cane-minore/quando: Evenings from January to March, highest in February at around 9 pm.
oggetti/cane-minore/dove: From Italy it is halfway up the sky towards the south, to the left of Orion. From the southern hemisphere it is halfway up the sky towards the north. Procyon forms the Winter Triangle with Betelgeuse and Sirius.
oggetti/cane-minore/come: With the naked eye; apart from Procyon it has no notable objects for binoculars.
oggetti/cane-minore/origine: Canis Minor is Latin for 'lesser dog'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/cane-minore/storia: In myth it is Orion's second hunting dog. For the Greeks what mattered most was Procyon, which rises shortly before Sirius.
oggetti/cane-minore/stelle/0/significato: From the Greek 'Prokyon', 'before the dog', because it rises before Sirius, the Dog Star. It is about 11 light years away.
oggetti/cane-minore/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the one with watery eyes'. It is a blue-white star.
oggetti/cane-minore/stelle/2/significato: A faint orange giant, close to Gomeisa.
oggetti/capricorno/cosa: A zodiac constellation shaped like a large triangle or a little boat. Its stars are not bright.
oggetti/capricorno/quando: Evenings from August to October, highest in September at around 9 pm.
oggetti/capricorno/dove: From Italy it is low in the south, below Aquila. From the southern hemisphere it passes high, almost overhead.
oggetti/capricorno/come: With the naked eye you can see that Algedi (alpha) is a pair of stars; with binoculars the pair is easy, and there is also the globular cluster M30.
oggetti/capricorno/origine: Capricornus is Latin for 'horned goat'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD), but the figure is much older, going back to the Babylonians.
oggetti/capricorno/storia: It is drawn as a goat with a fish's tail. A Greek myth tells that the god Pan, fleeing from the monster Typhon, dived into the river and became half fish. More than 2000 years ago the Sun was here at the winter solstice: hence the name Tropic of Capricorn.
oggetti/capricorno/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic for 'the goat's tail'. It is the brightest star in Capricornus.
oggetti/capricorno/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the luck of the butcher'. Binoculars show a fainter companion.
oggetti/capricorno/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic for 'the kid' (young goat). To the naked eye it forms a pair with alpha¹, but the two stars are at very different distances from us.
oggetti/capricorno/stelle/3/significato: From the Arabic for 'the bringer of good news'. It is next to Deneb Algedi.
oggetti/carena/cosa: A large constellation of the southern sky, very rich in stars. It contains Canopus, the second-brightest star in the night sky.
oggetti/carena/quando: It cannot be seen from Italy. From the southern hemisphere the best evenings are from February to April, highest in March at around 9 pm.
oggetti/carena/dove: From Italy it never rises: only Canopus can graze the horizon from the most southerly places. From the southern hemisphere it passes high in the south, crossed by the Milky Way, near the Southern Cross.
oggetti/carena/come: To the naked eye the Carina Nebula (NGC 3372) is splendid, a glowing cloud of gas that is even more beautiful through binoculars.
oggetti/carena/origine: Carina is Latin for 'keel', the keel of the ship. Until the 18th century it was part of the great ship Argo; Lacaille divided it into three parts in 1751-52 (Carina, Puppis and Vela).
oggetti/carena/storia: The Argo was the ship of Jason and the Argonauts, who set off to find the golden fleece. Inside the Carina Nebula lies Eta Carinae, a huge star that had a great outburst in the 19th century and for a few years became one of the brightest in the sky.
oggetti/carena/stelle/0/significato: Named after Canopus, the helmsman of Menelaus' ship in Greek myth. It is the second-brightest star in the night sky, and many space probes use it to find their bearings.
oggetti/carena/stelle/1/significato: A white star near the south pole of the sky; its name mixes Arabic and Latin.
oggetti/carena/stelle/2/significato: A modern name, given in the 1930s for a British navigation almanac. It is an orange star.
oggetti/carena/stelle/3/significato: From the Greek for 'little shield', the decorated shield on the stern of the ship Argo.
oggetti/centauro/cosa: One of the largest and brightest constellations in the southern sky. It contains Alpha Centauri, the star system closest to the Sun.
oggetti/centauro/quando: From Italy only the northern part can be seen, on evenings from April to June, highest in May at around 9 pm.
oggetti/centauro/dove: From Italy only its northern part can be seen, very low on the southern horizon, below Virgo; the finest part never rises. From the southern hemisphere it passes high, around the Southern Cross: alpha and beta are 'the Pointers' that show the way to the Cross.
oggetti/centauro/come: With the naked eye; the great globular cluster Omega Centauri (NGC 5139), the largest in the sky, looks like a fuzzy star, but from Italy it can only be seen from the South, skimming the horizon.
oggetti/centauro/origine: Centaurus is the centaur, half man and half horse. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/centauro/storia: It is often identified with Chiron, the wise centaur who taught heroes such as Achilles. He was accidentally wounded by one of Hercules' poisoned arrows and, unable to die, asked to give up his immortality.
oggetti/centauro/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic for 'the foot of the centaur'. Together with Toliman it forms Alpha Centauri, about 4.4 light years away: to the naked eye they look like a single star.
oggetti/centauro/stelle/1/significato: A very hot blue-white star, much farther away than Alpha Centauri.
oggetti/centauro/stelle/2/significato: The companion of Rigil Kentaurus, an orange star a little smaller than the Sun.
oggetti/centauro/stelle/3/significato: From the Arabic for 'the shoulder of the centaur'. It is an orange giant, and from Italy it can be seen low in the south.
oggetti/cefeo/cosa: A northern constellation shaped like a little house with a pointed roof. Its stars are not very bright.
oggetti/cefeo/quando: From Italy it never sets; it is highest on evenings from September to November, especially in October.
oggetti/cefeo/dove: From Italy it is high in the north, between Cassiopeia and the Pole Star. It cannot be seen from the southern hemisphere.
oggetti/cefeo/come: With the naked eye; binoculars show the 'Garnet Star' (mu Cephei), a deep red, and the variable star delta Cephei.
oggetti/cefeo/origine: Cepheus is the Greek name of King Cepheus. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/cefeo/storia: Cepheus was king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda. His star delta Cephei gave its name to the 'Cepheids', variable stars used to measure the distances of galaxies.
oggetti/cefeo/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic for 'the right arm'. It is a white star that spins very fast.
oggetti/cefeo/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the shepherd'. Because of the slow wobble of the Earth's axis, in about 2000 years it will be the pole star.
oggetti/cefeo/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic for 'the flock'. It is a blue star, slightly variable.
oggetti/cefeo/stelle/3/significato: An orange supergiant, close to the variable delta.
oggetti/balena/cosa: One of the largest constellations in the sky, but with dim stars. It represents a sea monster, long and stretched out below Pisces and Aries.
oggetti/balena/quando: Evenings from October to December, highest in November at around 9 pm.
oggetti/balena/dove: From Italy it is halfway up the sky towards the south, below Pisces and Aries. From the southern hemisphere it passes high in the sky.
oggetti/balena/come: With the naked eye; its most famous star is Mira (omicron Ceti), a variable that in about 11 months goes from easily visible to invisible without a telescope.
oggetti/balena/origine: Cetus is Latin for 'sea monster' or 'whale'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/balena/storia: It is the monster sent by Poseidon to devour Andromeda; Perseus killed it by showing it the head of Medusa, which turned it to stone. Mira was the first variable star of this kind to be discovered, in 1596: its name is Latin for 'wonderful'.
oggetti/balena/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic for 'the frog' (the second one; the first was Fomalhaut). It is an orange giant, the brightest star in Cetus.
oggetti/balena/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for the monster's 'nose'. It is a red giant.
oggetti/balena/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic for 'the tail'. It is an orange giant.
oggetti/balena/stelle/3/significato: From the Arabic for 'the cut-off hand'. Through a telescope it is a double star.
oggetti/camaleonte/cosa: A small constellation near the south pole of the sky, made of faint stars that form a small, elongated diamond.
oggetti/camaleonte/quando: It cannot be seen from Italy. From the southern hemisphere it is visible all year round, highest on May evenings.
oggetti/camaleonte/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere (Australia, South America) it never sets: it stays low towards the south, near the south celestial pole, below Carina.
oggetti/camaleonte/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky, far from towns; it has no easy objects for binoculars.
oggetti/camaleonte/origine: Chamaeleon comes from Greek and means 'chameleon'. It was introduced by the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman and published by Plancius at the end of the 16th century.
oggetti/camaleonte/storia: The Dutch navigators, on their way to the East Indies, gave the new southern constellations the names of exotic animals. On some old charts the chameleon seems to be sticking its tongue out towards nearby Musca, the Fly.
oggetti/camaleonte/stelle/0/significato: The brightest star, white. It has no proper name.
oggetti/camaleonte/stelle/1/significato: A red giant, faint but warm in colour.
oggetti/compasso/cosa: A tiny constellation of the southern sky: three small stars form a narrow triangle, like an open pair of compasses.
oggetti/compasso/quando: It cannot be seen from Italy. From the southern hemisphere the best evenings are from May to July, highest in June at around 9 pm.
oggetti/compasso/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere it passes high in the south, right next to Alpha Centauri.
oggetti/compasso/come: With the naked eye; it is easy to find because it sits next to Alpha Centauri, but it has no notable objects for binoculars.
oggetti/compasso/origine: Circinus is Latin for 'compasses', the kind used to draw circles. It was introduced by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in 1751-52.
oggetti/compasso/storia: Lacaille placed three drawing and measuring instruments side by side: Circinus (the Compasses), Norma (the Set Square) and Triangulum Australe (the Southern Triangle). He wanted to celebrate the instruments of the science of his day.
oggetti/compasso/stelle/0/significato: The brightest star, white. A small telescope shows a faint companion.
oggetti/compasso/stelle/1/significato: A white star, one of the points of the compasses.
oggetti/compasso/stelle/2/significato: A blue-white star, the other point of the compasses.
oggetti/colomba/cosa: A small winter constellation, below Lepus. Its brightest stars form a short, crooked line.
oggetti/colomba/quando: Evenings from December to February, highest in January at around 9 pm.
oggetti/colomba/dove: From Italy it is very low on the southern horizon, below Lepus and Orion. From the southern hemisphere it passes high, almost overhead.
oggetti/colomba/come: A dim constellation: you need a clear southern horizon and a dark sky; it has no easy objects for binoculars.
oggetti/colomba/origine: Columba is Latin for 'dove'. It was introduced by the Dutch cartographer Petrus Plancius at the end of the 16th century.
oggetti/colomba/storia: It is Noah's dove, which in the Bible returns to the ark with an olive branch to announce the end of the flood. Plancius drew it next to the great ship Argo.
oggetti/colomba/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic for 'the turtle dove'. It is a blue-white star, the brightest in Columba.
oggetti/colomba/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the weight'. It is an orange giant.
oggetti/colomba/stelle/2/significato: A yellow star in the dove's head.
oggetti/chioma-di-berenice/cosa: A small constellation between Leo and Arcturus. It has no bright stars, but under a dark sky you can see a cloud of little stars: this is the 'hair'.
oggetti/chioma-di-berenice/quando: Evenings from April to June, highest in May at around 9 pm.
oggetti/chioma-di-berenice/dove: From Italy it is very high, between the tail of Leo and Arcturus. From the southern hemisphere it is halfway up the sky towards the north.
oggetti/chioma-di-berenice/come: Through binoculars the Coma Star Cluster (Melotte 111) is lovely, a group of scattered little stars; with a telescope there are lots and lots of galaxies.
oggetti/chioma-di-berenice/origine: Coma Berenices is Latin for 'Berenice's hair'. It was already known in the 3rd century BC, but it became a constellation in its own right only in the 16th century, on the maps of Mercator and later of Tycho Brahe.
oggetti/chioma-di-berenice/storia: Berenice was a queen of Egypt: she offered her long hair to the gods so that her husband would come home safely from the war. The hair disappeared from the temple, and the astronomer Conon of Samos said the gods had placed it in the sky.
oggetti/chioma-di-berenice/stelle/0/sign: A star very similar to the Sun, fairly close to us.
oggetti/chioma-di-berenice/stelle/1/sign: From the Greek for 'diadem', the jewel in the queen's hair. Through a telescope it is a very close double star.
oggetti/chioma-di-berenice/stelle/2/sign: From the Arabic for 'the plait'. It is an orange giant at the centre of the cluster.
